The system uses a two-phase commit algorithm for transaction management and supports read-only transactions on replicas of the database.

answer.generated: To implement a deadlock detection mechanism in a distributed database system using Lamport clocks, one must first understand that Lamport clocks provide a way to order events in a distributed system chronologically. This ordering is crucial for detecting and resolving deadlocks, as it allows us to determine the sequence of operations and identify any circular wait conditions. In a distributed system managing customer orders across multiple servers, each server maintains its own Lamport clock to timestamp events. When a transaction starts, it increments the Lamport clock to mark the start of the transaction. During the execution of the transaction, all actions are timestamped with the current Lamport clock value. If a transaction needs to acquire a lock on a resource, it checks the Lamport clock values of other transactions holding locks on the same resource to ensure no circular wait condition exists. For instance, if transaction T1 holds a lock on resource R1 and T2 holds a lock on resource R2, and both attempt to acquire each other's lock, the system can detect a potential deadlock by comparing the Lamport clock values. If T1 requests a lock from T2 after T2 acquired its lock, and vice versa, a deadlock is likely. The system then employs a deadlock detection algorithm such as the Banker's algorithm or a simple timeout mechanism to resolve the deadlock by aborting one of the transactions and rolling back its changes. This approach ensures that all transactions complete successfully, maintaining the integrity and consistency of the distributed database.
